questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Suitable Variation of Parameters Ansatz
questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=({x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2x).
$$

According to the method of variation of parameters, which of the following is a suitable ansatz for the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3y=1-4x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-3x})}^{′}+3(u{e}^{-3x}) & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3u{e}^{-3x}+3u{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}}+\cancel{3u{e}^{-3x}} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-3x} & =1-4x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{3x}(1-4x) \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-3x} \\  & =\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-3x} \\  & ={e}^{-3x}\int {e}^{3x}(1-4x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+7y={e}^{-7x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+7{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-7x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-7x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-7x})}^{′}+7(u{e}^{-7x}) & ={e}^{-7x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-7x}-7u{e}^{-7x}+7u{e}^{-7x} & ={e}^{-7x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-7x}-\cancel{7u{e}^{-7x}}+\cancel{7u{e}^{-7x}} & ={e}^{-7x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-7x} & ={e}^{-7x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-7x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-7x} \\  & =x{e}^{-7x}.\end{aligned}
$$
